title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Purpose

This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs), error budget policies, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. It is intended as the single source of truth for service owners and SREs who are responsible for production reliability and capacity.

Scope

- Applies to all externally customer-facing inference services (Redwood API, Dedicated endpoints, and provisioning control planes) and internal infrastructure that impacts customer-facing SLOs (routing, cache layer, KV store, GPU pools).
- Excludes experimental research clusters and ephemeral developer sandboxes unless flagged for production traffic.

Document outline

1) SLO definition and template
2) Error budget policy and burn controls
3) Capacity planning process and formulae
4) Reliability initiatives (OKRs / projects)
5) Incident review standards and templates
6) Operational tooling and observability requirements
7) Runbook library: template and examples

1) SLO definition and template

Overview

- SLOs describe the expected reliability of a customer-facing capability in terms that map to user experience (e.g., request success rate, p95/p99 latency for inference, embedding throughput). SLOs tie to SLAs and commercial commitments where applicable.

Standard SLO fields (use this template for every service):

- SLO id: short-dash-name (e.g., inference-text-generation-availability)
- Service owner: team name / primary oncall alias
- User-facing metric: success_rate | latency_ms | throughput_rps | data_consistency
- Measurement window: rolling 30d (default) / 7d for high-churn services
- Target: percentage or latency threshold (string) e.g., "99.95% success over 30d" or "p99 latency < 1.2s (token stream disabled)"
- SLO rationale: business impact and why target chosen (one paragraph)
- Primary alerting rule: link to metric alert (pager duty escalation)
- Error budget policy: rate of allowed violations and burn actions (link to section 2)
- Owner and reviewers: list of stakeholders and quarterly reviewers

Example SLOs (canonical):

1. inference-generation-availability:
   - metric: success_rate (HTTP 2xx)
   - target: 99.95% over 30d
   - rationale: protect synchronous API experience for paid customers

2. inference-generation-latency-p99:
   - metric: p99 end-to-end latency (ms) for non-streaming text generation calls (seq <= 1024)
   - target: p99 < 1200ms over 30d
   - rationale: latency is correlated with abandonment and product conversion

3. embeddings-throughput:
   - metric: median tokens/s per inference node and queue depth
   - target: 99% of requests served without queueing > 200ms

SLO review cadence

- Every SLO must be reviewed at least quarterly. The owner is responsible for updating the SLO rationale when product changes (new feature flags, model quantization, dedicated capacity introduced).

2) Error budget policy and burn controls

Definitions

- Error budget = 1 - SLO_target (for availability SLOs expressed as %).
- Budget burn = observed violations consuming the error budget over the measurement window.

Default policies (apply unless a customer-specific SLA overrides):

- Green (<= 25% budget used in last 7d): normal operations, changes can proceed as standard.
- Yellow (25% < used <= 60%): owner notified, reduce risky rollouts; require scaled canaries and increased monitoring for deployments.
- Orange (60% < used <= 90%): freeze dangerous changes (no schema migrations, no infra rollbacks unless safety), require pre-approval from SRE lead and runbook rehearsals for planned changes.
- Red (> 90% used): immediate mitigation steps, open an incident bridge if ongoing, rollback recent risky changes, engage product & legal if customer impact is significant.

Operational responses (numbered steps):

1. Automated detection: metric alert triggers when 25% budget used in last 7d (email + slack).
2. Owner notification: owner acknowledges within 1 business hour with an initial plan.
3. Mitigation: implement short-term mitigations (e.g., scale up nodes, enable cache bypass, reduce batching) within 2 hours for Orange/Red.
4. Post-mortem: when error budget crosses 60% or an incident opens, a blameless post-mortem is required within 7 days.

3) Capacity planning process and formulae

Goals

- Ensure production clusters have headroom to meet SLOs under expected load and planned growth while optimizing cost.

Inputs

- Current 95th percentile load (RPS or tokens/s)
- Growth forecast (monthly %) and planned product events (launches, promotions)
- Observed utilization per node (GPU/CPU/RAM) and service-specific saturation metrics (KV IO, disk QPS)
- Planned changes (models with different memory/compute profiles, quantization rollout)

Planning cadence

- Quarterly planning for major capacity purchases and monthly operational refreshes for autoscaling policies.

Headroom formula (example for GPU-backed inference clusters):

- effective_capacity_per_node = baseline_inference_throughput * (1 - safety_margin)
- required_nodes = ceil( projected_peak_load / effective_capacity_per_node )

Where:
- baseline_inference_throughput = measured tokens/s sustained on a representative workload
- safety_margin = 0.25 default (25%) for production pools; increase to 40% for SLA-backed Dedicated pools

Example calculation:

- measured tokens/s = 100k tokens/s across cluster
- project_growth = 30% expected peak in 3 months -> projected_peak_load = 130k tokens/s
- baseline_per_node = 10k tokens/s -> effective_capacity = 10k * (1 - 0.25) = 7.5k
- required_nodes = ceil(130k / 7.5k) = 18 nodes (plan to provision 20 nodes to meet rollout flexibility).

Autoscaling and burst capacity

- Configure autoscaling policies with both scale-up threshold (e.g., sustained 70% GPU util for 3 min) and scale-down cooldowns (10 minutes) to avoid oscillation.
- Maintain a small burst reserve pool (2-3 nodes per availability zone) for sudden traffic spikes; these can be pre-warmed instances with optimized model weights.

4) Reliability initiatives (OKRs / projects)

Objective examples (annual / quarterly):

- O1: Reduce p99 inference latency by 15% across top 3 models (Owner: serving-runtime)
  - Key results: kernel opt rollout to all GPU instances, dynamic batching improvements +15% throughput, identify and fix top 5 tail-latency hot paths.

- O2: Improve error budget stability for the API product (Owner: eng-sre)
  - Key results: reduce mean time to mitigation from 90m to 30m, reduce frequency of emergency rollbacks by 50%, operationalize automated runbook actions for top 3 incident classes.

Project playbook for reliability initiative:

1. Define measurable KPI (metric & target) and baseline.
2. Create a cross-functional project with owner, PM, QA, and SRE representatives.
3. Schedule a canary and staged rollout plan with explicit rollback criteria.
4. Instrument additional metrics and create dashboards/alerts.
5. Run experiments in staging and ramp to production if success criteria met.

5) Incident review standards and templates

Principles

- Blameless: focus on systemic causes, not individuals.
- Timely: incident review initiated within 48 hours of incident closure; final report within 7 days for severity >= Sev2.
- Action-driven: each postmortem must include 1+ corrective actions with owners and due dates.

Severity definitions (short):

- Sev1: Customer-facing outage with broad impact or SLA breach; 24x7 engagement and immediate remediation.
- Sev2: Significant degradation affecting subsets of customers or critical workflows; requires SRE and product engagement in business hours.
- Sev3: Minor degradation or non-customer impacting internal issues.

Incident review template (to paste into the postmortem):

- Incident title:
- Severity:
- Start time / End time (UTC):
- Impact summary (customer-visible impact):
- Detection method (alert, customer report, internal monitoring):
- Timeline (detailed):
- Root cause(s):
- Short-term mitigation details and timeline:
- Long-term remediation actions (owner + due date):
- Error budget impact (quantify):
- Lessons learned and follow-ups:

Quality gates for postmortems:

- Must be reviewed by SRE lead and product owner before closure.
- Must link to runbooks and alerts that triggered; if none existed, create runbook as part of remediation.

6) Operational tooling and observability requirements

Minimum observability for any SLO-backed service:

- Metrics: request rate, success rate (2xx/available), error classes (4xx/5xx with service-side error breakdown), latency p50/p95/p99 by route and model, queue depth, GPU util, memory pressure.
- Distributed tracing: automatic sampling of 100% for requests with errors, 1% sample for regular traffic (adjustable).
- Logs: structured JSON logs with request_id, route, model, shard, and trace_id; retention 30 days for default, longer for SLA-backed customers (configurable).
- Dashboards: per-SLO dashboards accessible to owner and SRE; include budget burn view, traffic heatmap, and node utilization.
- Alerts: SLO burn thresholds, latency SLO breaches, infrastructure saturation (GPU memory > 85%), and noise-reduction rules (alert aggregation).

Operational tools list (approved):

- Metrics store: Prometheus + Thanos (long-term)
- Tracing: Jaeger (local) / Tempo in prod
- Logging: ELK stack (Elastic) + Graylog for urgent stream analysis
- Incident management: PagerDuty + shared incident Slack channel (#incidents)
- Runbook store: Confluence runbook pages (this system)
- Capacity planning: internal spreadsheet templates + Terraform state for provisioning
- Chaos and resilience testing: Chaos Toolkit + periodic game-days

7) Runbook library: template and examples

Runbook template (copyable):

- Runbook title: short service-action (e.g., inference-api-high-queue-depth)
- Owner: team or oncall alias
- Symptoms: bullet list of observable signs (e.g., p95 latency > 1s and request queue depth > 200)
- Immediate checks (ordered):
  1. Verify alert timeline and confirm metric values (link to dashboard).
  2. Check recent deploys in last 2 hours: `git log` / orchestration UI.
  3. Check autoscaler events and node health: `kubectl get nodes` or fleet console.
  4. Validate model-serving processes and GPU memory: `ps` / `nvidia-smi` on targeted nodes.
- Short-term mitigations (ordered with commands):
  1. Scale up inference pool by +2 nodes (Terraform / cloud provider CLI) with pre-warm hook.
  2. Disable batching for critical routes: update ConfigMap `batching.enabled=false` and roll config via canary.
  3. Bypass cache to avoid cache-stampedes: toggle route flag.
- Long-term remediation ideas:
  - Tune dynamic batcher parameters (max_batch_size, timeout_ms) and re-run perf test suite.
  - Improve KV cache strategy: move hot prefixes to dedicated cache shard.
- Runbook validation and rehearsal schedule: must be rehearsed at least once per quarter for top 5 runbooks.

Canonical runbook examples (links):

- inference-api-high-latency -> /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-inference-api-high-latency
- gpu-pod-oom -> /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-gpu-pod-oom
- kv-store-degraded -> /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-kv-store-degraded

Governance and ownership

- Every SLO must have an assigned owner who is responsible for reviews, actioning error budget escalations, and maintaining runbooks.
- eng-sre is the central arbiter for SLO policy changes; engineering teams may propose SLO adjustments with evidence.

Onboarding checklist for new service owners

1. Create SLO using the template above and register it in the SLO registry (Confluence index + metrics dashboard).
2. Attach runbooks for top 3 incident classes.
3. Create dashboards and configure alerts with appropriate noise suppression.
4. Walk through runbooks with SRE and perform a runbook rehearsal.

Appendices

A) Standard alert thresholds (examples)

| Metric | Threshold | Severity |
|---|---:|---|
| Availability (30d) | < 99.95% | Sev1 |
| p99 latency (inference) | > 1200ms | Sev2 |
| GPU util | > 90% sustained 10m | Sev2 |
| Queue depth | > 200 requests | Sev2 |
| Error rate (500s) | > 0.5% of requests | Sev2 |

B) Quick command references

- Check recent deploys: `kubectl rollout history deployment/inference-api`
- Scale pool (example): `terraform apply -var='pool_size=20' -target=module.inference_pool`
- Inspect a node: `ssh node-123 'nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv'`

C) Change history

- 2026-02-20: Published initial standard. Author: Ari Chen.
- 2026-03-04: Updated error budget burn thresholds and added runbook rehearsal requirement. Reviewers: Maya Patel, Diego Ramirez.

If you have questions or suggested updates, add comments to this page or contact eng-sre@redwood.example.com.
